name: Jackbox Games
subcategory: party games for a room full of phones
tagline: Party game packs where one screen hosts and everyone plays from their phone browser at jackbox.tv.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Sold as one-time game purchases on stores rather than a monthly plan.

verdictSummary: The technical part of Jackbox is genuinely small: a host screen, a four-letter room code, phones joining a web page, a websocket relay, and a timer. An agent can build a working prompt-and-vote party game in one sitting and it will be fun the first night. What it cannot build is the thing you actually paid for: thousands of hand-written prompts, the voice acting, the music stings, the art direction, and the fact that your friends already know the rules of Quiplash. You end up with an engine and an empty content library, which means you are now the writers' room. Great weekend hack, bad replacement for pack night.
coreLoopDIY: Runs a local host screen that shows a room code while phones join over the LAN and play rounds of write-a-prompt-answer then vote, with scoring and a winner screen.
requirements: Node.js on a laptop plugged into the TV
everyone on the same wifi, or a tunnel service if remote
a screen to share if you play over video call
your own prompt list, which is the actual work
whatYouLose: The writing: thousands of tested prompts, jokes, and fill-in-the-blanks that took professional comedy writers years
Voice acting, music, transitions, and art that make the whole thing feel like a TV show instead of a form submission
Thirty-plus distinct games including drawing, trivia, bluffing, and drawing-adjacent chaos, not just one loop
Audience mode for dozens or thousands of extra viewers, plus the streaming-safe filters
Zero-setup joining: guests type a code on a phone and it works, no LAN caveats, no explaining what a tunnel is
Console and TV builds so it works without a laptop wrangler
moatNotes: The room-code trick was never the product. The product is a comedy writing staff plus fifteen years of knowing which prompts make a living room laugh.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because thirty dollars once buys a night where nobody has to explain anything. The games are pre-written, pre-tested, and pre-known by at least one person in the room, the audio does the emotional work, and the failure mode of your DIY version is a silent group staring at a text box waiting for someone to be funny with no scaffolding. Jackbox is a content purchase wearing a software costume, and content does not clone in one prompt.
notes: Build the engine for fun, then discover that writing 200 good prompts is harder than writing the websocket layer.
prompt:
Build a local-network party game host, in the style of a phone-controller quiz show, in an empty folder.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Node.js 20 with TypeScript, Express for static files, the ws package for websockets
- Zero database: all game state lives in memory in the server process
- Frontend: plain HTML, CSS, and vanilla TS compiled to one bundle per screen. No React, no Tailwind.

Two screens:
1. Host screen at / : shows a four-character room code, the LAN join URL, a QR code for it, the connected player list, then the current round state and scores. Meant for a TV.
2. Player screen at /play : name entry plus room code, then a single big input or vote buttons depending on round phase.

Game loop, exactly one game mode called "Zinger":
- 3 to 8 players, minimum 3 to start
- Each round: every player gets a text prompt from prompts.json and 60 seconds to type an answer
- Then all players vote on the funniest answer for each prompt they did not write
- Points for votes received, double points on the final round, then a winner screen with confetti
- Host screen drives all timers; players just react

Requirements:
- Server picks a random unused room code, one room at a time is fine
- Handle reconnects by name so a phone locking the screen does not kill the game
- Print the LAN join URL on boot by reading the machine's non-loopback IPv4
- prompts.json ships with 30 example prompts and a comment saying write your own, this is the actual work
- No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry, no analytics. If any config is needed use .env with a .env.example.

Out of scope: drawing games, audience mode, audio, remote play over the internet, mobile app, persistence between sessions.

Deliver: README with npm install, npm run dev, and how to add prompts. Make the host screen legible from ten feet away.
